en: Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The *Buddhabhāṣita-duḥkhaskandha-sūtra*, translated by an unknown person, is now appended to the Later Han Record.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the monks had all gathered together after midday for a discussion on some minor matter.

Then, certain followers of other paths and different doctrines were wandering about after midday when they came to where those monks were. Having arrived, they exchanged greetings with the monks, and having exchanged greetings, they sat down to one side.
When those followers of other paths and other teachings had sat down to one side, they said to the bhikṣus:
“Venerable sirs!
The śramaṇa Gautama speaks with wisdom regarding sensual desire; he speaks with wisdom regarding form and sensation.”
"Venerable friends!
We too speak of sensual desire through wisdom, and we speak of form and feeling through wisdom.
Venerable friends!"
"In what way is there a difference, in what way is there an inferiority, and in what way is there a distinction? This ascetic Gautama and we are both possessed of wisdom.
At that time, having heard what the followers of other paths and heterodox teachers had said, the bhikṣus neither approved nor disparaged it.
Having neither approved nor disparaged it, he rose from his seat and departed, thinking:
"Now that I have heard this teaching and questioned the World-Honored One, I shall fully understand its meaning."
He then went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arrival, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down to one side.
Once those bhikṣus were seated to one side, they related in full detail to the Blessed One everything that had been discussed among them with the followers of other paths and other schools.
Having spoken thus to the Blessed One, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Bhikṣus! At that time, one should speak in this way to those of other paths and other teachings:"
"What is the flavor of sensual desire?
What is its decay? What is its abandonment?"
What is the scent and flavor of form?
What is its decay? And what is its abandonment?
What is the flavor of sensation?
What is its decay?
What is its relinquishment?
"O bhikṣus! You should answer in this way.
When those of other paths and other teachings hear this, they will look at one another with hostility and seek further debate; they will certainly become angry."
Filled with resentment and anger, he remained silent; his countenance was displeased, his limbs were soiled, and he turned his back toward the speaker, unable to respond.
Distorting his face, he rose from his seat in silence and immediately departed.

Why is this? Because among the gods, the world, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—including all devas and humans—I do not see anyone who, upon hearing what I have spoken, understands its meaning as I do, whether they have heard it from the Tathāgata, from a disciple of the Tathāgata, or from someone else who has heard it here.
What is the flavor of sensual pleasure?
It refers to the pleasure or joy that arises because of the five types of sensual indulgence.
Such is the flavor of sensual pleasure; herein there is much ruin and decay.
"What is the ruin caused by sexual misconduct?

This son of good family may sustain his life through various crafts or skills—whether by farming, trading, serving as a hired scribe, studying arithmetic, studying calculation, studying poetry, studying *śloka* meters, teaching writing, or responding to official recruitment. Driven by cold when it is cold and driven by heat when it is hot, he endures hunger and thirst, and is bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas; he endures all this in order to seek wealth."
That son of good family exerts himself in such a way, practices in such a way, and applies himself with such diligence.

Yet, despite acting in this manner, he fails to obtain wealth and property; consequently, he becomes sorrowful and unhappy, weeping, beating his own breast and striking himself, and out of delusion speaks these words:
"I have acted foolishly; I have failed to obtain it."
That clansman, not allowing [distractions] to arise, diligently practices his conduct and thereby attains the fruit.
Having obtained wealth, he guards it, stores it away securely, thinking:
"May this wealth of mine not be seized by the king, may it not be stolen by thieves, may it not be burned by fire, may it not rot and decay, and may I not suffer loss on my investments."
Though he guards his wealth, it is seized by the king, stolen by thieves, or consumed by fire and thus destroyed; he seeks profit but fails to obtain it.
He then becomes sorrowful and dejected, weeping and wailing; he beats his own breast and strikes himself, further increasing his delusion.

Furthermore, that which he has long cherished and delighted in is now ruined, destroyed, and lost. This present body is a mass of suffering, caused by sensual desire, conditioned by sensual desire, and dominated by sensual desire; it is the causal condition of sensual desire.

Sentient beings, with lust as their cause, lust as their condition, and lust as their predominant influence, quarrel because of lust: mother quarrels with son, son quarrels with mother; father quarrels with son, son quarrels with father; elder brother quarrels with younger sister, younger sister quarrels with elder brother.

They engage in mutual strife and contention; the mother speaks of the son's faults, and the son speaks of the mother's faults; the father speaks of the son's faults, and the son speaks of the father's faults; the elder brother speaks of the younger sister's faults, and the younger sister speaks of the elder brother's faults—how much more so among ordinary people?
This is the present mass of suffering, caused by lust, conditioned by lust, and dominated by lust.

Because of lust, conditioned by lust, and dominated by lust, these beings quarrel: kings quarrel with kings, brahmins quarrel with brahmins, householders quarrel with householders, and low-caste artisans quarrel with low-caste artisans; each engages in mutual strife and each prepares various weapons for combat.

Whether with fists, or stones, or knives, or clubs, one undergoes the suffering of death within them; this is the present mass of suffering caused by sensual desire, conditioned by sensual desire, and dominated by sensual desire.
Due to lust, and due to excessive lust, these sentient beings don armor, take up bows and arrows, or don leather armor and carry extremely sharp swords, surrounding one another in a massed battle.

In that regard, they may engage in combat with elephants, or with horses, or with chariots, or with infantry; or they may engage with women, or with men. Among these, there may be death or the suffering of dying. This is the present mass of suffering caused by sensual desire, conditioned by sensual desire, and dominated by sensual desire.

Because of lust, and because of excessive lust, these beings don armor and take up extremely sharp swords; they go to a very high city with the intent to attack it. Therein, some blow conch shells, some beat drums, some raise their voices in shouts;

others use mallets, or halberds, or axes, or sharp wheels, or shoot arrows at one another; others drop boulders from above, or discharge crossbows, or pour molten copper upon them. They die therein, suffering the pain of death; this is the aggregate of suffering manifest in the present, arising from lust and from excessive lust.

Because of lust, and due to excessive lust, these sentient beings go to royal cities and towns; they may break through walls or plunder treasuries, steal the property of others, or block their paths. They destroy cities and ravage villages, killing other people. Seized by the authorities, they are forced to undergo various forms of suffering:

some have their heads cut off, some have their hands and feet cut off, some have their ears cut off, some have their noses cut off, some have both their ears and noses cut off, some have their topknots cut off, some have their hair cut off, and some have both their topknots and hair cut off.
Some are placed inside wooden chests; some are killed by being crushed under clothing; some are placed upon sand and stones; some are placed upon grass;
some are placed within the mouths of iron donkeys; some are placed within the mouths of iron lions; some are placed inside copper cauldrons;
some are placed inside iron cauldrons; some have their bodies cut into pieces; and some are pierced with sharp forks.
Or they lie upon beds of hot iron with boiling oil poured over them; they are placed in mortars and pounded with iron pestles;
or they are bitten by dragons, beaten with clubs, or rolled up like mats;
then, brought beneath a banner, their heads are severed with swords—this is the mass of suffering in the present body, arising from lust and, in particular, from excessive lust.

Because of lust, and even because of excessive lust, these beings engage in bodily austerities and verbal and mental austerities. At that time, if they fall ill and suffer, lying on a bed, sitting on a seat, or reclining in the shade, their bodies experience extreme pain and intense agony; they find no joy and desire to end their lives.

That is to say, because of those ascetic practices of body, speech, and mind, at the time of death he is suspended head-downward; it is like the sun about to set behind a great mountain range in the twilight, its shadow hanging downward.
Thus, having practiced such bodily austerities, verbal austerities, and mental austerities, when his life ended, he was suspended upside down.
He thought to himself:

"I have practiced these bodily, verbal, and mental austerities while suspended upside down, yet I originally performed no meritorious deeds and created no merit. I committed many evils—namely, acting wickedly, acting greedily, and acting violently; I performed no meritorious actions, no wholesome deeds, nor did I perform any acts that lead to a favorable rebirth. I shall surely fall into a woeful state."

This leads to regret; having regretted, it is unwholesome both at its conclusion and in its arising. This is a mass of suffering in the present, caused by sexual desire and culminating in excessive sexual desire.

Because of lust, and because of excessive lust, these beings engage in bodily asceticism and verbal and mental asceticism. Having performed such bodily and mental asceticism, when their bodies perish at death due to those causes and conditions, they are reborn in the miserable states, in the hells.
This is the mass of suffering that constitutes his body; because of lust, and due to the intensification of lust, it is called the ruin caused by lust.
"What is the abandonment of lust?
If one has a seeking desire for lust, one should cease that seeking desire and transcend lustful craving; abandoning this lustful craving is what is meant by the abandonment of lust."

"Among those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who thus relish sensual desire, there is within them a state of corruption; they abandon it without knowing it as it truly is. How could they possibly abandon sensual desire themselves?"
Furthermore, can it also stop others?
For instance, if it coexists with abiding, how could it possibly stop lust? This is not the case.

Regarding those ascetics and brahmins who thus perceive the flavor of sensual desire as something that leads to ruin, and who are able to renounce it knowing it as it truly is, it is possible that they themselves will later cease from sensual desire and can also cause others to cease, so that both they and those with whom they dwell are able to cease from sensual desire. This is indeed possible.
"What is the color of the flavor?

It is when a woman of the kṣatriya caste, a woman of the brāhmaṇa caste, a woman of the artisan caste, or a woman of the commoner caste—whether fourteen or fifteen years of age—is at that time fully endowed with beauty; at that time, her physical form possesses both pleasure and joy."
At that time, among these odors, tastes, and forms, there is much decay and ruin.
What is the decay of form?

It is like seeing a sister who has grown old and senile, whose years have passed, whose teeth have fallen out and hair has fallen away, whose back is bent like a tortoise shell, and who walks while leaning on a staff and stretching her limbs.
"What do you think?
Would that former beautiful appearance not eventually decay?
"Indeed it would, World-Honored One!"

"Furthermore, one should regard it as seeing a sister suffering from illness: whether she lies upon a bed, or sits upon a seat, or lies in the shade, with pain pervading her entire body, in extreme agony and distress, finding no joy and wishing for life to end."
"What do you think?
Would that former beautiful appearance not eventually perish?
"Indeed it would, World-Honored One!"
"Furthermore, it is as if one were to see a sister who has died for one day up to seven days, being pecked by crows or hawks, eaten by dogs or foxes, burned by fire, buried, or infested by worms."
"What do you think?
Would that former beautiful complexion not eventually perish?
"Indeed it would, World-Honored One!"
“Furthermore, suppose one were to see the corpse of a sister—whether as bones, or as bluish, or as infested with worms, or as being devoured, or as white bones.
What do you think?”
“Would that former beautiful complexion not surely perish?
“Indeed it would, World-Honored One.
“Furthermore, if one sees the corpse of a sister, with neither skin nor flesh remaining, but only tendons connecting the bones.”
"What do you think?
Would that former beautiful complexion not eventually decay?
"Indeed it would, World-Honored One!"

"Furthermore, if one sees the corpse of a sister, with her bones and joints disarticulated and scattered in various places—the foot-bones in one place, the shoulder-blades, the thigh-bones, the hip-bones, the spinal column, the shoulder-bones, the neck-bones, and the skull-bone each in a separate place."
"What do you think?
Would that former beautiful appearance not eventually decay?
"Indeed it would, World-Honored One!"
"Furthermore, if one sees a corpse that has become like a sister—its bones as white as a conch shell, or the color of a blue pigeon, or reddish and oily, or decayed and crumbling."
"What do you think?
Would that former beautiful complexion not eventually decay?
"Indeed it would, World-Honored One!"
"This is the disintegration of form.
How does one abandon form?
It means that regarding form, there is seeking and desire; one should cease such seeking and desire, transcend all seeking and desire, and thus abandon this form."

"Regarding those ascetics and brahmins who thus experience the taste for form, yet within which that form is subject to decay, and who neither relinquish it nor know it as it truly is—how could they possibly bring form to a halt?"
Furthermore, can one stop another?
If one dwells together with them, how could one possibly stop form? This is not so.

Whichever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas know this taste and form as subject to decay, and having known it as it truly is, abandon and relinquish it—they are able to cease form themselves and can also cause others to cease it. That those who dwell thus are able to cease form is indeed possible.
"What is the flavor of sensation?

Here, a bhikṣu is liberated from sensual desires and dwells in the attainment of the four dhyānas. While dwelling therein, he neither harms himself nor harms others; being thus unharmed, he attains bliss within that state."
Why is this? I have said that by being free from ill-will one attains pleasant feeling; this is the gratification of feeling.
"What is the ruin of feeling?"
That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to cessation—this is the decay of feeling.
"What is the relinquishing of feeling?
It is the seeking of desire for feeling; to cease that seeking of desire and to transcend that seeking of desire is the relinquishing of feeling."

“If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas do not understand the decay of such sensations and their associated feelings, do not know how to relinquish them, and do not know them as they truly are, how could they possibly bring an end to suffering for themselves?”
Furthermore, can one also cause others to cease [suffering]?
To say that one dwells together with those who have abandoned suffering is not possible.

However, among those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding such sensations of craving, know them to be subject to decay and thus abandon them, knowing them as they truly are—such persons can cease their own suffering and can also cause others to cease it; for it is possible that one who dwells together with them may likewise be able to cease suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and were delighted.
*The Sūtra on the Aggregate of Suffering* preached by the Buddha.
